blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Alternating Current : An alternating Current is one whose direction reverses periodically.

Equation for I and V

$I=I_0 \sin \omega t \quad \text { or } \quad I=I_0 \cos \omega t$

$\mathrm{I}=\text { Instantaneous value of current at time } \mathrm{t} \text {, }$, $\mathrm{I}_0=\text { Amplitude or peak value }$

Instantaneous Values : The instantaneous value is "the value of an alternating quantity at a particular instant of time in the cycle."

Peak value/Maximum value:  The maximum value of alternating quantity (I or V) is defined as peak value. It may or may not be equal to amplitude.

Average Value: The mean value of A.C. over any half cycle (either positive or negative) is that value of DC which would send same amount of charge through a circuit as is sent by the AC through same circuit in the same time.

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{avg}}=<\mathrm{I}>=\dfrac{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \text { Idt }}{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{\text { Area under I-t graph }}{\text { time interval }}$

Note:

(a) Since average value of AC over complete cycle is zero therefore, batteries cannot be charged by using ac.

(b) Electrolysis and electroplating cannot be done by using ac.

Physical significance of Average Current :

$\therefore \text { Charge flown by DC of value } \mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{av}}=\text { Charge flown by } \mathrm{AC} \text { of value } \mathrm{i}$

Root Mean Square (RMS) value of current: It is value of DC which would produce same heat in given resistance in given time as is done by the alternating current when passed through the same resistance for the same time.

$I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} I^2 d t}{\int_{t_1}^{t_2} d t}} \text { or } I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\left\langle I^2\right\rangle$

AC ammeter and voltmeter reads RMS value of current and voltages respectively.

$\Rightarrow i_0>i_{r m s}>i_{a v}$

Important Note :

(1) The r.m.s. value of alternating current is also called virtual value or effective value.

(2) In general when values of voltage or current for alternating circuits are given, these are r.m.s. value.

(3) AC ammeter and voltmeter always measure r.m.s. value. Values printed on ac circuits are r.m.s. values.

(4) In our houses ac is supplied at 220 V, which is the r.m.s. value of voltage. It's peak value is  $\sqrt{2} \times 220=311 \mathrm{~V}$

Note: Alternating current and voltages are measured by a.c. ammeter and a.c. voltmeter respectively. Working of these instruments is based on heating effect of current, hence they are also called hot wire instruments.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Phasor Diagram:- A diagram representing alternating current and voltage (of same frequency) as vectors (phasor) with the phase angle between them.

Properties :

(1) They rotate anticlockwise

(2) The length of phasors represents the maximum value (amplitude) of quantity.

(3) Vertical component represents its instantaneous value.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Resonance: A circuit is said to be resonant when the natural frequency of circuit is equal to frequency of the applied voltage. For resonance both L and C must be present in circuit.

(a) At Resonance

$\text { (i) } \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}$

$\text { (ii) } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{C}}$

$\text { (iii) } \phi=0 \text { (V and I in same phase) }$

$\text { (iv) } \mathrm{Z}_{\min }=\mathrm{R} \text { (impedance minimum) }$

$\text { (v) } \mathrm{I}_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{R}} \text { (current maximum) }$

(b) Resonance frequency

$\because \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}} \Rightarrow \omega_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{~L}=\frac{1}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{C}} \Rightarrow \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2=\frac{1}{\mathrm{LC}} \Rightarrow \omega_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{LC}}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{2 \pi \sqrt{\mathrm{LC}}}$

(c) Variation of Z with f

$\text { (i) If } \mathrm{f}<\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{r}} \text { then } \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}<\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text { circuit nature capacitive, } \phi \text { (negative) }$

$\text { (ii) At } \mathrm{f}=\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{r}} \text { then } \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text { circuit nature, Resistive, } \phi=\text { zero }$

$\text { (iii) If } \mathrm{f}>\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{r}} \text { then } \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}>\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text { circuit nature is inductive, } \phi \text { (positive) }$

(d) Variation of I with f:As frequency (f) increases, impedance (Z) first decreases, then increases. Current (I) first increases, then decreases.

At resonance, the impedance of a series resonant circuit is minimum, acting as an "acceptor circuit" because it allows maximum current at its natural frequency.

In radio/TV tuning, we match the circuit frequency to the desired station’s frequency to receive it.

Half Power Frequency:- There are two such frequencies of applied ac-source in LCR-series circuit where power consumption is exactly half of the maximum at resonance such frequencies are called half power frequencies.

$\begin{aligned} & \text { At } \omega_1 \& \omega_2 \Rightarrow P=\frac{P_{\max }}{2} \quad I=\frac{I_{\max }}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \omega_2-\omega_1=\frac{R}{L} \Rightarrow 2 \Delta \omega=\frac{R}{L} \end{aligned}$

Quality factor or Q-factor:-

$\begin{aligned} Q  &= \frac{\omega_0}{\text{Bandwidth}} = \frac{\omega_0}{2 \Delta \omega} \\ \text{Since } \Delta \omega &= \frac{R}{2L}, \quad \text{then} \quad Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_0 R C} \\ Q &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{LC}}} \times \frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}} \Rightarrow Q = \frac{1}{R} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{C}}} \end{aligned}$

Q - factor  $\propto$ Sharpness

According to figure, if 'R' is decreasing means Q-factor or sharpness will increase in the circuit.

Average power :

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~V}_0 \mathrm{I}_0 \cos \phi \quad or \quad \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos \phi \quad or \quad P_{a v}=\left(\frac{V_{r m s}}{2}\right)^2 \times R  \quad or \quad P_{a u}=I_{r m s}^2 R$

Note : Hence $\cos \phi=\frac{R}{Z}$ = Power factor of AC Circuit

Average power in capacitive circuit $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=0$

Average power in Inductive circuit $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=0$

RMS Power: $P_{r m s}=V_{r m s} I_{r m s}$

Wattless current: That component of current in ac-circuit which is not active. Hence, $\operatorname{I} \cos \phi$ is the activity component of current because it is in phase with applied voltage. But $\operatorname{I} \sin \phi$ is the component which is inactive, called as wattless current because it is in $\frac{\pi}{2}$ phase with applied voltage.

Power factor :

$\cos \phi=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{Z}}$

1. Watt full Power: Average power is also known as watt full power

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos \phi$

2. Watt less Power: That component of current in ac-circuit which is not active.

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{rms}} \sin \phi$

Choke Coil:- It is used to control alternating current without any power loss. It is an inductor and low resistance.

A choke coil, with minimal resistance, is used to control current in an AC circuit.

The power loss in the choke :

$P_{a v}=V_{\text {rms }} I_{r m s} \cos \phi \rightarrow 0$

$\cos \phi=\frac{r}{Z}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+\omega^2 L^2}} \approx \frac{r}{\omega \mathrm{~L}} \rightarrow 0$

Note: A capacitor of suitable capacitance replace a choke coil in an AC circuit, the average power consumed in a capacitor is also zero. Hence, like a choke coil, a capacitor can reduce current in AC circuit without power dissipation. Cost of capacitor is much more than the cost of inductance of same reactance that's why choke coil is used.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Confusing Average and RMS: The average value of a sinusoidal AC is zero, but the RMS value is non-zero and used for power calculations.

2. Incorrect Formulas: Using wrong formulas, such as applying the average formula for RMS or vice versa. Use:

3. Not Considering Waveform Type: Applying sinusoidal formulas to non-sinusoidal waveforms like square or triangular waves.

4. Using Peak Values Directly: Forgetting to convert peak values to RMS or average values. For sinusoidal:

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Confusing Impedance with Resistance: Treating impedance (Z) as simple resistance (R), ignoring phase differences.

2. Incorrect Phase Angle: Not accounting for the phase difference between voltage and current in reactive components.

3. Misunderstanding Phasors and Complex Numbers: Errors in converting between phasor form and time-domain expressions.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Ignoring Resonance Condition: Not recognizing that resonance occurs when inductive and capacitive reactances cancel each other.

2. Incorrect Resonant Frequency Calculation: Miscalculating the resonant frequency using the wrong formula.

3. Overlooking Bandwidth: Failing to understand the role of bandwidth and quality factor (Q).

4. Assuming Ideal Components: Ignoring real-world component resistances affecting resonance.

5. Misunderstanding Phase Relationship: Incorrectly assuming voltage and current are always in phase at resonance.
